headline: Dinosaurs never went extinct—they evolved into birds and are all around us
universal_truth: Endings can be transformations; what seems to disappear may simply change form
fun_facts: The closest living relatives of T. rex are chickens and ostriches
Feathered dinosaurs have been found in fossils—many dinosaurs had feathers, not scales
There are about 10,000 bird species alive today—more than all other dinosaur lineages that went extinct
discussion_questions: How does knowing birds are dinosaurs change how you see them?
What other 'extinct' things might have simply transformed?
Why did only the bird lineage of dinosaurs survive?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Dinosaurs didn't go extinct 66 million years ago. One lineage survived, evolved, and thrived. You see them every day—pecking at seeds, flying overhead, singing in trees. Birds are dinosaurs. The terrible lizards never left.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Birds seem so different from the dinosaurs we picture—no massive size, no teeth, covered in feathers. How do we know birds really are dinosaurs and not just their descendants?
cliff.prompt: How do we know birds are dinosaurs?

options.text: Birds share unique skeletal features with theropod dinosaurs and fossil evidence shows the transition
options.response: Yes. Hollow bones, wishbones, feathers, hip structure—birds have dinosaur anatomy. Fossils show feathered dinosaurs, and the transition to birds was gradual.

options.text: DNA analysis shows birds evolved from dinosaurs
options.response: We can't get dinosaur DNA, but skeletal evidence is definitive...

q1.title: Feathered Fossils
q1.script: Fossils from China show dinosaurs covered in feathers—not for flight, but perhaps for warmth or display. Feathers evolved before flight. T. rex may have had feathers as a juvenile. The scaly dinosaurs of movies are partly fiction.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Feathered Fossils"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Chicken Rex
q2.script: The closest living relatives of Tyrannosaurus rex are chickens and ostriches. Protein analysis from T. rex bones showed similarities to bird proteins. Your backyard chicken is a miniature, modified version of the king of predators.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Survival Story
q3.script: When the asteroid hit 66 million years ago, most dinosaurs died. But small, feathered, flying dinosaurs survived—and diversified into 10,000 bird species. The extinction was real; the lineage persisted through transformation.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Endings can be transformations. What seems to disappear may simply change form. Dinosaurs didn't end—they evolved. This pattern repeats: many 'extinctions' are actually transformations in disguise.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 138. Tomorrow, we'll explore life under water. Until then, watch a bird and remember: you're looking at a living dinosaur.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Dinosaur Spotting - See the Living Past
growTrack.activity: Watch a bird today—any bird. Notice its movements, its body, its feathers. You're looking at a dinosaur—a direct descendant of creatures that walked with T. rex. 66 million years of evolution, still alive and flying around you.
